parole.testo: From Old Swedish abbot, abot, abbote, abote, from Latin abbās, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Doublet of abbé.
From Latin acacia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía).
From Latin acrībia, from Ancient Greek ἀκρίβεια (akríbeia). Attested since 1929. Cognate of German Akribie, Italian acribia.
From Old Swedish antikrister, from Latin antichristus, from Ancient Greek ἀντίχριστος (antíkhristos), equivalent to anti- + Kristus.
From Latin antithesis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), equivalent to anti- + tes. Cognate of German Antithese, French antithèse.

parole.significato: Apocrypha, apocryphal work (writings recognized by some but not all Christians)
parole.testo: Via Late Latin from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden”), from ἀποκρύπτειν (apokrúptein, “to hide”), from ἀπό- (apó-) + κρύπτειν (krúptein). Related to krypta, krypto-.
From Latin apologeticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós). First attested in 1816.

parole.significato: pharmacy (a place where prescription drugs are dispensed)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Old Swedish apotek, from Latin apotheca (“storehouse”), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of butik.
From Latin Aramaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἀραμαῖος (Aramaîos).
From Latin Arcas, Arcadis, from Ancient Greek Ἀρκάς (Arkás), Ἀρκάδος (Arkádos) + -ier.
Borrowed from Latin archīāter, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιατρός (arkhiatrós), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἰατρός (iatrós).
Borrowed from Latin arcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós).
Borrowed from Latin asphaltus, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos).
Borrowed from Latin asthenia, from Ancient Greek ἀσθένεια (asthéneia).
From Latin aula, from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”). First attested in 1846.
Borrowed from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of aria.

parole.significato: authentic, authentical, real (not fake or forgery), reliable, trustworthy, really originating from the person or time i…
parole.testo: Cognate with German authentisch, English authentic and authentical, French authentique, from Latin authenticus and Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós), used in Swedish since 1755.
Inherited from Old Swedish balsam, from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon), likely from a Semitic source. Compare Hebrew בֹּשֶׂם (bōśem, “perfume”) and Arabic بَشَام (bašām).
Borrowed from Latin beryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos). Doublet of brillor and briljant.

parole.significato: to test software prior to release
parole.testo: Latin bēta, from Ancient Greek βῆτα (bêta).
From Latin blasphemia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía).
From Late Latin cystis (“cyst”), from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “bladder”).
Borrowed from Latin decalogus, from Ancient Greek δεκάλογος (dekálogos). First attested in 1738.
From Medieval Latin dæmonizo, from Ancient Greek δαιμονίζομαι (daimonízomai). Attested since 1887, rare until the 1990s.
From Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”).
From Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos, “servant”). Doublet of djäkne.

parole.significato: a discus (plate-like object that is thrown)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos).
From Latin dogma, from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma).
Latin oecūmenicus < Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós, “from or open to the whole world”).
Via Latin elephantus from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās); replaced Old Swedish fīl (“elephant”), Old Norse fíll.
Borrowed from Latin empyreum, from empyrius, derived from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (whence Swedish fyr (“fire”)). First attested in 1871.
Borrowed from Late Latin epenthesis, from Ancient Greek ἐπένθεσις (epénthesis).
Derived from Late Latin epidemia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδημία (epidēmía).
epikuré + -isk, from Latin epicureus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικούρειος (epikoúreios), from Ancient Greek Ἐπίκουρος (Epíkouros). Cognate of German epikureisch.
From Latin Esseni, from Ancient Greek Ἐσσηνοί (Essēnoí).

From Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “relating to customs or character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “custom, character”), from earlier ἒθος (èthos). Possibly related to sed (“custom”).
Borrowed from Latin aetiologia, from Ancient Greek αἰτιολογία (aitiología).

Ultimately from Latin Europaeus, Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos). Likely through German Europäer; compare older Swedish europeer, europäer as singular form. For the building type compare aramé, farisé.
Borrowed from Latin eurhytmia, from Ancient Greek εὐρυθμία (euruthmía).
From Latin phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνῐξ (phoînĭx).
From Late Latin phrasis, from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis).
Derived from Latin physiognōmia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμίᾱ (phusiognōmíā).

parole.significato: jet (a very black form of coal)
parole.testo: From Latin gagates and Ancient Greek γαγάτης (gagátēs), cognate with German Gagat, used in Swedish since 1747.

parole.significato: Galilean (pertaining to the Galilee region in the Middle East)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin galīlaeus, from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαῖος (Galilaîos).
Derived from Latin galīlaeus, from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαῖος (Galilaîos).
From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos).
Inherited from Old Swedish glosa. Borrowed from Latin glossa. Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă). According to SO attested since circa 1600.
Medieval Latin, from Latin halos, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon”). Related to English and Danish halo.
Borrowed from Latin hebraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hecticus, from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός (hektikós), from the noun ἕξις (héxis, “state of mind, habit”).
Borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis).
From Latin haereticus (from Ancient Greek αἱρετῐκός (hairetĭkós)) + -er.
From Latin haereticus (from Ancient Greek αἱρετῐκός (hairetĭkós)) + -isk.
Borrowed from Latin Hermaphroditus, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμαφρόδιτος (Hermaphróditos). Cognate of German Hermaphrodit.
Borrowed from Latin homilia, from Ancient Greek ὁμιλία (homilía).
Borrowed from Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ). Doublet of hyperbel.
Derived from Late Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós).
From Latin hysterica, from hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). Attested since 1914.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin īdōlatrīa, from Late Latin īdōlolatrīa, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολατρίᾱ (eidōlolatríā, “worship of idols”).

parole.significato: an idyllic place or circumstance, an idyll
parole.testo: From Latin idyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion). Cognate with Danish idyl, English idyll and German Idyll, used since 1781. Doublet of idé and idol.
Borrowed from Latin chaldaeus, from Ancient Greek Χᾰλδαῖος (Khăldaîos).

From New Latin camera obscura (literally “dark chamber”), because the first cameras used a pinhole and a dark room; from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”). Doublet of kam
From Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, “vast chasm, void”).
From Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτη (khártē). Doublet of kort, from Old Norse kort (“a map”), and cert.
Derived from Latin catechesis, from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis).
From Latin catecheticus, from Ancient Greek κατηχητικός (katēkhētikós), equivalent to kateket + -isk.
From Latin catechumenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos).
Derived from Latin Celtae, from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí).
Borrowed from Latin cenotaphium, from Ancient Greek κενοτάφιον (kenotáphion).
Borrowed from Latin centaurus, from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros).
From Latin chirurgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).

parole.significato: surgery (a procedure involving major incisions to remove, repair, or replace a part of a body)
parole.testo: From Latin chirurgia, from Ancient Greek χειρουργία (kheirourgía).

parole.significato: surgical (of, relating to, used in, or resulting from surgery)
parole.testo: From Latin chirurgicus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργικός (kheirourgikós).
From Latin cholericus, from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “bile, gall”). Compare German Choleriker.
From Latin cholericus, from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “bile, gall”). Compare German cholerisch, French cholérique.
Borrowed from Late Latin colophon, from Ancient Greek κολοφών (kolophṓn, “top, point, end”).
From Latin cōlon, from Ancient Greek κῶλον (kôlon).

Borrowed from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós). Originally used by Herodotus in reference to giant statues in Ancient Egyptian temples. Cognate of Danish kolos, German Koloss, French colosse.
From Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma), from κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).
Ultimately from Latin cuprum, from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros, “Cyprus”).
Borrowed from Latin coriandrum, from Ancient Greek κορίανδρον (koríandron), alternative form of κορίαννον (koríannon).
From Latin cranium, from Ancient Greek κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”), used in Swedish since 1798.
From Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).
From Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē). Doublet of korona and corona.
Derived from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Doublet of kryptisk, krypto, grift, grotta, and grotesk.
Borrowed from Latin Croesus, derived from Ancient Greek Κροῖσος (Kroîsos). First attested in 1770. Cognate with English Croesus, French Crésus, and German Krösus.
Borrowed from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβύρῐνθος (lăbúrĭnthos, “a maze”).
From Late Latin liquiritia, alteration of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza), from γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”).

parole.significato: Levite (member of the Hebrew tribe of clergymen)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Levītēs, from Ancient Greek Λευῑ̈́της (Leuī̈́tēs).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin litania, letania, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía).

parole.significato: a container for transportation of liquids, e.g. a wooden barrel or a ceramic flagon
parole.testo: From Old Swedish läghil, from Latin lagoena, lagēna, lagūnaλᾰ́γῡνος, from Ancient Greek λᾰ́γηνος (lắgēnos), λᾰ́γῡνος (lắgūnos). Compare Medieval Latin lagula, lagella. Borrowed from Latin magia, derived from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía). First attested in 1674.

parole.significato: a Macedonian (person from the Republic of Macedonia)
parole.testo: From Latin mācedonus, mācedonicus, from Ancient Greek μακεδόνιος (makedónios), from μακεδών (makedṓn) + -ιος (-ios), equivalent to Makedonien + -ier.

From Old Swedish marmor(sten), from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros), perhaps related to μαρμαίρειν (marmaírein, “to gleam”). First attested in the early 15th century (in the compound marmorsten).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

Borrowed from Latin mausōlēum, from Ancient Greek Μαυσωλεῖον (Mausōleîon) from Ancient Greek Μαύσωλος (Maúsōlos); named for Mausolus (Μαύσωλος or Μαύσσωλλος), satrap of the Persian empire and ruler of Caria.
From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros).
Derived from Latin Mēdus, from Ancient Greek Μῆδος (Mêdos). Cognate of German Meder, French mède.
Derived from Late Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).
From Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).
Borrowed from Latin metamorphōsis, from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis). Cognate of English metamorphosis, French métamorphose, German Metamorphose.
Borrowed from Latin metathesis, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: a method (process by which a task is completed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).
From Latin methodicus, from Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós). Morphologically analyzable as metod + -isk. Compare German methodisch, French méthodique.
From Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), μόναρχος (mónarkhos).

parole.significato: a monarchy (form of government with a hereditary head of state)
parole.testo: From Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía).
Derived from Latin Maurus, possibly from Ancient Greek μαυρός (maurós). Compare origin of morian, mauretanier.
Borrowed from Latin mystērium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion). Doublet of mystär. Cognate with German Mysterium.
Borrowed from Latin Nāïas, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás).

parole.significato: Neapolitan (pertaining to the Italian city of Naples)
parole.testo: From Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεᾱ́πολῐς (Neā́polĭs).
From New Latin narcoticum (an ellipsis of remedium narcoticum), neuter of narcoticus, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτικός (narkōtikós). Doublet of narkotisk.
Derived from Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis). Cognate of German Oase, English and French oasis.
From Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra), from Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale”). Attested since 1640.
Borrowed from Latin ophthalmia, from Ancient Greek ὀφθᾰλμῐ́ᾱ (ophthălmĭ́ā), from ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmós).
From Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).
From Latin Orphicus, from Ancient Greek Ὀρφικός (Orphikós), suffixed with -ism. Compare German Orphismus, French orphisme.
From Latin Orphicus, from Ancient Greek Ὀρφικός (Orphikós).
Derived from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis).
From Old Swedish ostra, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon).
Derived from Latin paragraphus, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos). Cognate of English paragraph, French paragraphe, German Paragraph.

parole.significato: parallel (of two or more (straight) lines, (flat) surfaces etc: equally distant from one another at all points)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin parallēlus, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos).

parole.significato: a parallelogram (convex quadrilateral in which each pair of opposite edges are parallel and of equal length).
parole.testo: From Latin parallēlogrammum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλόγραμμον (parallēlógrammon), neuter of παραλληλόγραμμος (parallēlógrammos, “limited by parallel lines”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos) + γραμμή (grammḗ).
From Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περῐπᾰτητῐκός (perĭpătētĭkós).
From Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs).
From Ecclesiastical Latin polemicus, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós), from Ancient Greek πόλεμος (pólemos). Attested since 1773. Compare French polémique, German polemisch.

parole.significato: forecast, prognosis (prediction of the future course, or outcome, of a situation)
parole.testo: pro- + -gnos, borrowed from Latin prognōsis, from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσις (prógnōsis, “foreknowledge, perceiving beforehand, prediction”), from prefix προ- (pro-, “before”) + γνῶσις (gnôsis, “inquiry, investigation, knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”).
Derived from Medieval Latin prognōsticō, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós).
From Latin prōnōmen, from pro- + nomen, a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντωνυμία (antōnumía).
From Latin proselytus, from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos). First attested in 1734.
From Latin psalmodia, from Ancient Greek ψαλμῳδία (psalmōidía).
Borrowed from Latin pȳthon, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn).
From Latin rheumatismus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós, “humour, discharge, rheum”), cognate with English rheumatism, French rhumatisme and German rheumatismus.
From Latin rūta, from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).
From Latin Sadducæi, from Ancient Greek Σαδδουκαῖοι (Saddoukaîoi).
From Latin sapphīrus (“saphire”), from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros).
From Latin septicus, from Ancient Greek σηπτικός (sēptikós).

parole.significato: sesame (tropical Asian plant Sesamum indicum and its seed).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēsamum, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon); see there for more.
Borrowed from Latin sphaera, from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra).
Derived from Late Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).
Borrowed from Latin Sīrēn, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn).

parole.significato: a dinosaur (animal belonging to the clade Dinosauria)
parole.testo: From skräck (“horror, terror”) + ödla (“lizard”). Calque of New Latin dīnosaurus, from Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “terrible, awesome, mighty, fearfully great”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard, reptile”).
From Latin scythicus, from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs).
Inherited from Old Swedish smaragd, from Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), from a Semitic language.
Borrowed from New Latin spasmōdicus, from Ancient Greek σπασμώδης (spasmṓdēs, “spasmodic”), from σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”).
Borrowed from New Latin staphylococcus, from Ancient Greek σταφυλή (staphulḗ) + κόκκος (kókkos). Cognate of German Staphylokokkus, French staphylocoque.
From New Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós).

parole.significato: stigma (an indication of infamy or disgrace)
parole.testo: From Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark of slavery or disgrace”).
Derived from Latin stōicus, from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós). Cognate of German Stoiker.
Derived from Latin strategus, from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós).

parole.significato: a strap, a strop (to attach to (in the form of a loop), for restraining, pulling, hanging, or the like)
parole.testo: Originally a naval term. Cognate of English strop, strap, Dutch strop. Likely from the same root as strupe. Possibly from Latin stroppus, from Ancient Greek στρόφος (stróphos).

parole.significato: Stygian (of, by or relating to the river Styx in Greek mythology)
parole.testo: Likely from Latin stygius, from Ancient Greek Στύγιος (Stúgios, “relating to Styx”), from Στύξ (Stúx, “Styx, chief river of underworld”). First attested in 1723. Compare English Stygian and German stygisch. Corrosive sense from the belief that the River Styx contained corrosive water.
Borrowed from Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).
Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ).
Borrowed from Latin synecdoche, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ).
Borrowed from Late Latin synodus, from Ancient Greek σύνοδος (súnodos, “meeting, astronomical conjunction”), from συν- (sun-) + ὁδός (hodós).
Borrowed from Latin synodicus, from Ancient Greek συνοδικός (sunodikós). By surface analysis, synod + -isk.
Derived from Latin syringa, from syrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx), likely due to the hollow branches of the plant. Cognate of Danish syren.
Used in Swedish since 1748. Cognate with Danish syzygie, German Syzygie, from Late Latin syzygia and Ancient Greek σύζυγος (súzugos, “yoked together”).
From Latin theo-, from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-).

parole.significato: a thesis, a statement, a hypothesis, a doctrine, an idea, a thought, a theory
parole.testo: From Latin thesis and Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis, “a proposition, a statement”), used in Swedish since 1664.
Borrowed from Latin thrombosis, from Ancient Greek θρόμβωσῐς (thrómbōsĭs).

parole.significato: to occupy an elevated or prominent position (literally or figuratively), such as on a throne
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trona, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “chair, throne”). By surface analysis, tron (“throne”) + -a (used to form verbs).
From New Latin oedema, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”).
